title: Step 1 integration tests: long-running task simulation (wait-or-defer + single-flight)
description: Integration tests (NO mocks; real test workflow) simulating a workflow with a deliberately LONG-running command. Build a test workflow/command whose _process_command sleeps longer than wait_seconds (configurable) to deterministically simulate the ~10-min LLM call. Assert: (1) a turn exceeding wait_seconds returns a deferred response (running + turn_key) WITHOUT orphaning the execution; (2) a retry with the same args returns the SAME turn_key and starts NO second execution (assert the long command body runs exactly once, e.g. via a call counter/log); (3) the execution still completes and persists after the request returned; (4) §3.3: a retry arriving before /initialize startup completes receives exec_state=running + startup_turn_key, never an empty startup_output; (5) the fast path returns the result inline when the command is quick; (6) no ctx mutation outside runtime.lock; (7) process_message DeprecationWarning no longer emitted. Follow tests/ conventions (integration only).
notes:
TEST SCOPE NARROWING (per user): Test ONLY /initialize with a startup_action so NO workflow training is required (no trained intent models needed — a startup_action dispatches a command directly by name, bypassing NLU/intent detection). Build/extend a small test workflow with a command whose _process_command sleeps for a configurable duration to simulate the long-running LLM call. Drive everything through POST /initialize (startup_action -> submit_turn(kind='initialize_startup')). Concretely assert: (1) FAST PATH — when the startup command is quick (sleep < wait_seconds), /initialize returns 200 inline with startup_output + exec_state=DONE; (2) DEFER — when sleep > wait_seconds, /initialize returns 202 with startup_turn_key + exec_state=running WITHOUT orphaning the execution; (3) SINGLE-FLIGHT RETRY (§3.3) — a second /initialize for the same channel arriving before startup completes hits the 'already exists' branch and returns the SAME startup_turn_key + exec_state=running (NEVER an empty startup_output), and the sleeping command body runs EXACTLY ONCE (assert via a call counter / log); (4) the deferred execution still completes and persists after the request returned; (5) the process_message DeprecationWarning is no longer emitted. Skip the /invoke_agent and /invoke_assistant agent-path assertions here (those require trained models) — cover them separately if/when training fixtures exist.
WORKFLOW TEMPLATE (per user): The hello_world example is a good template for the small test workflow. See tests/hello_world_workflow/ (and fastworkflow/examples/hello_world/) — a minimal application/ + _commands/ pair (e.g. add_two_numbers.py with a Signature.Input/Output + ResponseGenerator). Clone that structure into a new fixture (e.g. tests/long_running_workflow/) and make the command's _process_command sleep for a configurable duration (read from the Input params or an env var) to simulate the long LLM call. Because the test drives it via /initialize startup_action (direct dispatch by command name), no plain_utterances/generate_utterances/training is needed — the Signature can be minimal. Reuse the existing tests/ conftest fixtures and conventions.
close_reason: tests/test_fastapi_turns_async.py: fast-path inline, defer+single-flight (one execution across retries), pointer-based 409. Driven via /initialize startup_action against tests/hello_world_workflow (no training). Full suite 457 passed.

title: DiskSessionStateStore key is not injective: two channels can share one pending blob
description:
DiskSessionStateStore._json_path folds separators: channel_id.replace(os.sep,'_').replace('/','_') + '_pending.json'. So channel ids 'tenant/user-1' and 'tenant_user-1' map to the SAME file. Whichever suspends second overwrites the first, and the first user's suspended conversation is silently replaced by a stranger's.

This is the same defect class the checkpoint store already fixed. fastworkflow/checkpoint_store.py encodes channel keys injectively (percent-encoding, with a hash tail beyond the filesystem name limit) precisely so two channels cannot share storage, and keeps the raw channel_id inside the record so a collision quarantines instead of cross-serving.

SEVERITY. Cross-session state exposure, not just loss: user A can be handed user B's suspended trajectory, which carries the ReAct trajectory and any ask_user answers in it. Reachable wherever channel ids are structured (tenant/user, org/team/user) -- a common shape for multi-tenant deployments.

DISCOVERED FROM fix-6b4 while adding iter_entries(). The reaper sidesteps it by reading channel_id from INSIDE the blob rather than parsing the filename (see test_channel_id_comes_from_the_blob_not_the_filename), so retention is correct regardless. The underlying collision is untouched.

FIX. Reuse the checkpoint store's encoding rather than inventing a second one -- ideally lift it into a shared helper so the two stores cannot drift. Needs a migration or read-both-shapes window for blobs already on disk under the old name.

NOT urgent for single-tenant deployments with opaque channel ids (uuids collide only on equality). Urgent for anyone using path-shaped ids.
close_reason:
Fixed. encode_path_component was lifted out of checkpoint_store.py into a new shared fastworkflow/storage_keys.py that both stores import, so the pending store now keys through the same injective percent-encoding the checkpoint store already used -- one encoder, two callers, no room to drift. tenant/user-1 and tenant_user-1 can no longer share a blob, and neither can ids differing only by case (uppercase is escaped, which matters on APFS/NTFS even though it is invisible on ext4).

THE SUBTLE PART, and it is load-bearing: the new suffix is '.pending.json', not '_pending.json'. Verified directly -- the old folding maps tenant/a to 'tenant_a_pending.json', and the new encoder maps the literal id tenant_a to 'tenant_a' too, so had the suffix been kept a NEW-form read for tenant_a would have landed on tenant/a's LEGACY blob. The original bug would have survived inside its own fix. Differing at position -13 makes a legacy name unable to equal a new name.

Legacy window: load/exists fall back to the old name, and the legacy read verifies the channel_id INSIDE the blob because the old name was shared by every id that folded onto it -- that field is the only remaining evidence of ownership. save() writes only the new name and unlinks the superseded legacy copy (without which one channel gets two iter_entries rows and the reaper ages out the wrong one); clear() removes both. Removable once every deployment has run longer than PendingRetentionPolicy.max_age_seconds (7 days); the five sites are listed on _legacy_json_path's docstring.

17 tests in tests/test_pending_state_keys.py. Nine-mutation matrix, no survivors.

DISCOVERED AND FILED: fix-3xf (empty channel_id now 500s at the storage layer instead of 400ing at the API boundary -- better than the old behaviour, which gave every empty id one shared file, but failing in the wrong place) and fix-xm1 (reap can increment reclaimed for a blob whose embedded channel_id does not map to its own filename; pre-existing).

Doc rot from the fix: docs/turn_result_design.md corrected (filename, and it still claimed default=str, removed back in v2.26.0). The two adversarial-review documents still describe the collision as live and were deliberately left alone -- they are dated review records, and editing them would falsify the provenance.

title: Redact secrets and PII from persisted session state
description:
Deferred from the serialization-hook design (docs/fastworkflow_serialization_hooks_design.md section 6.2), adjudicated 2026-08-05 as decision 4 of that design. Discovered from fix-qyz.

WHY THIS EXISTS. The accepted persistence model (decision 25 of the memory-bounds design, as modified) is persist-all-JSON-native BY DEFAULT. Whatever an author puts in workflow.context therefore reaches disk in the clear when a session is checkpointed. Today serialize_state() does not persist workflow.context at all, so this exposure is NEW and arrives with Release B.

What can end up there: api keys, refresh tokens, cookies, signed URLs, database credentials, a nested bearer token, and secrets a user typed into an ask_user prompt that the ReAct trajectory then retained. PII has the same problem and is not covered by any key-name heuristic at all.

INTERIM POSITION (shipped with the hook design, not a substitute for this work): author-facing documentation says do not attach secrets or PII to command contexts or workflow context, and do not inject them into agent trajectories, without strong encryption.

ONE EXCLUSION IS NOT DEFERRED. fastWorkflow injects the caller's JWT into application context itself - _merge_workflow_context (run_fastapi_mcp/utils.py:253) and _update_http_bearer_token (:260) both set workflow.context["http_bearer_token"]. Persisting that would be the framework writing a credential IT added, which no amount of author documentation addresses. That single key is excluded from the default projection as part of the hook work, not here.

SCOPE WHEN THIS IS PICKED UP:
- A default deny-list over credential-shaped key names at any depth. Starting list from the design draft: api_key, apikey, access_key, secret, secret_key, password, passwd, token, access_token, refresh_token, bearer, authorization, credential, credentials, private_key, session_key, cookie, signature. Case-insensitive on normalised names.
- Drop by name; log at DEBUG BY NAME ONLY, never by value; absent on restore rather than restored as None, so an author cannot mistake a redacted value for a real one.
- Extension point: Serialization.redact in _commands/_serialization.py may ADD to the deny-list but not remove from it.
- Decide whether drop-and-log is the right default or whether a credential-shaped key should refuse the whole projection (pin the session) instead.
- The ReAct trajectory is a separate and harder surface than workflow.context: a secret supplied as an ask_user answer lives in the trajectory blob, not under a named context key, so the deny-list does not reach it. Decide whether trajectory persistence needs its own treatment or whether awaiting sessions simply stay pinned (see decision 26 of the memory-bounds design, which already pins them for Release B v1).

STATE THE LIMIT HONESTLY WHEN THIS SHIPS. A key-name deny-list catches conventionally-named keys. It does not catch a credential stored under user_data, one embedded in a URL string, or one inside a trajectory. It is a safety net, not a guarantee, and the release notes must say so in those words rather than implying the data is protected.
notes:
SCOPE EXTENDED 2026-08-05: this issue now also owns the optional author-facing ENCRYPTION extension point, not just redaction. Reason: both answer the same question - what to do about sensitive values an author has chosen to persist - and designing them in two passes would produce two mechanisms with one purpose.

PROPOSED SHAPE: optional `encrypt` / `decrypt` classmethods on `class Serialization` in _commands/_serialization.py, alongside `redact`.

THE CONDITION THAT DECIDES WHETHER IT IS PROTECTION OR THEATRE: the key must not travel with the ciphertext. A framework-managed key sitting beside the data it protects is the "encrypted at rest, key on the same disk" anti-pattern - it moves an audit checkbox without moving the exposure. Real protection means envelope encryption with a key from the deployment's KMS or secret manager, which fastWorkflow should INTEGRATE WITH rather than mandate or own. Do not reuse the JWT signing key: it couples two concerns and widens that key's blast radius.

NOT IN SCOPE HERE - http_bearer_token. It was considered for encryption and rejected, because encrypting it would preserve a value that should not be preserved at all. It is request-scoped data living in a session-scoped container: every authenticated request re-supplies it (get_session_and_ensure_runtime passes that request's own token at __main__.py:250, and ensure_user_runtime_exists refreshes it on the existing runtime). Persisting it is unnecessary (the next request supplies a fresh one), actively harmful (a restored value is stale by construction, may be expired, and can overwrite the fresh token the current request just installed), and already forbidden by non-negotiable rule 2 of the memory-bounds design. It is excluded from the default projection as part of the hook work (fix-qyz), not encrypted here.

NORMATIVE GUIDANCE THIS WORK SHOULD PUBLISH, in priority order:
1. A credential that arrives with a request belongs to that request. Re-supply it per request; never checkpoint it. This is the first-line norm and it removes the problem instead of managing it.
2. Do not attach secrets or PII to contexts or inject them into agent trajectories at all.
3. Only when state is BOTH genuinely long-lived AND genuinely secret, encrypt it - with an external key, per the condition above.
Leading with encryption would teach the wrong lesson: it normalises persisting secrets when the better answer is usually not to.

title: Design the workflow serialization hook mechanism (needs approval before implementation)
description:
BLOCKS all Release B persistence work. Adjudicated 2026-08-05 as part of the fix-g03.13 decision gate. Design only - do NOT implement until Dhar has reviewed and approved the design.

WHAT CHANGED. Decision 25 as written in the memory-bounds design said "nothing is durable by default; a workflow declares what may be persisted". That is REVERSED. The accepted decision is: persist all JSON-native context BY DEFAULT, and expose hooks so the application developer can extend or override serialization.

REQUIREMENTS (from the adjudication):
1. Hooks let an app developer EXTEND or OVERRIDE serialization of their own state.
2. Warn when a workflow that needs a hook has not implemented one.
3. An explicit NO-OP implementation must NOT warn. A no-op is the author's signal that they know about the requirement and have chosen nothing - silence is consent, absence is not.
4. The mechanism must follow well-known, established patterns for serialization hooks rather than inventing a bespoke one.
5. Dhar reviews and approves the design before any implementation.

SCOPE IS WIDER THAN CONTEXT DICTS. The hook is not only for overriding context-dict serialization. It is also the mechanism that makes a workflow EVICTABLE AT ALL, because what pins a session is the live command-context object (TodoListManager, the WorkItem tree) which is not JSON-native and which persist-all cannot reach. Decision 18's resolution depends on this hook existing. Design it for both jobs.

PRIOR ART TO EVALUATE (the design should justify its choice against these, not pick one silently):
- Python native: __getstate__ / __setstate__ (the pickle protocol's state hooks, usable without pickle), __reduce__, copyreg.
- Registry/converter style: cattrs structure/unstructure hook registration, marshmallow and DRF schema classes registered per type.
- Framework-declarative: pydantic model_serializer / model_validator; Django natural_key.
- JVM/.NET: Serializable + writeObject/readObject, Externalizable, ISerializable.
REPO-NATIVE IDIOM: context classes already expose optional classmethods discovered through CommandContextModel.get_context_class(..., ModuleType.CONTEXT_CLASS) - get_parent and get_displayname are existing examples (workflow.py:219-234, :186-196). A serialization hook following that same discovery path would be consistent with what workflow authors already write, and would let the framework detect "declared but no-op" vs "absent" cleanly, which requirement 3 needs.

MUST ALSO ADDRESS - credential exposure. Persist-all moves the data-classification boundary: an unrestricted Workflow.context can hold api_key, refresh tokens, cookies, signed URLs, DB credentials, a nested http_bearer_token, or a secret a user typed into an ask_user prompt that is retained in the ReAct trajectory (design section 11.1). A warning only protects a deployment if somebody reads logs. The design should propose a default redaction pass over credential-shaped keys/values in addition to the warning, so the loud default is not the only guard. Subject to the same review.

DELIVERABLE: a design document for review covering the hook signatures and discovery, versioning of the declaration, the declared/no-op/absent trichotomy and its warning behaviour, how identity-preserving and cyclic structures are handled (the WorkItem tree has parent back-references and an identity-keyed _child_pos map), the redaction proposal, and the failure mode when a hook raises.
notes:
DESIGN WRITTEN, AWAITING REVIEW (2026-08-05). Document: docs/fastworkflow_serialization_hooks_design.md (uncommitted). Do not implement until approved.

PROPOSED MECHANISM, in one paragraph: the author implements optional classmethods on the `class Context` in `_commands/<ContextName>/_<ContextName>.py` - the same file and discovery path that already carries `get_parent` and `get_displayname`. The pair is `get_state(obj) -> dict | fastworkflow.EPHEMERAL` and `from_state(state, workflow) -> obj`, chosen because every established pattern surveyed (pickle `__getstate__`/`__setstate__`, cattrs structure/unstructure, Django `natural_key`/`get_by_natural_key`, Java `Externalizable`, .NET `ISerializable`) converges on a dump plus a class-side factory. It is NOT a dunder on the application class, because that would change `pickle` and `copy` semantics for the author's own class.

THE TRICHOTOMY (requirement 3) resolves on METHOD PRESENCE, which is the only positive signal available: absent method -> pin + warn; method returning `fastworkflow.EPHEMERAL` -> pin, no warn (the declared no-op); method returning a dict -> evictable. A method returning `None` is treated as a bug: pin AND warn, with a message saying to return EPHEMERAL if declining was intended.

FINDING THAT SHAPED THE DESIGN: surveying the five pinned workflows, THREE of five (simple_workflow_template, todo_list_workflow, messaging_app_4) move `current_command_context` to a node INSIDE a graph the framework did not build, and messaging_app_3 sets `current` with NO root at all. So identity inside a restored graph is the normal case, not a corner. The design therefore serializes a single anchor (root if set, else current) and stores the other two context slots as LOCATORS relative to it, via an optional `get_locator`/`find_by_locator` pair, with a serialize-time self-check that `find_by_locator(anchor, get_locator(obj)) is obj`. Two independent snapshots of the same node would restore as two objects and break the invariant that current is a node inside root.

REDACTION (requirement 6, added here): a framework default deny-list over credential-shaped key names at any depth, dropped by name, logged at DEBUG by name only, absent rather than None on restore, extendable via `Serialization.redact`. Explicitly documented as a safety net and not a guarantee - it does not catch a credential under an unconventional key name, inside a URL string, or in a ReAct trajectory.

FIVE DECISIONS ARE OPEN for the review, listed in section 12 of the document: hook naming and placement; the locator pair as a separate hook vs one all-slots hook; what a version mismatch does (quarantine vs discard); the redaction deny-list and whether drop-and-log is the right default; and whether `_commands/_serialization.py` should exist as a new optional module type.

All code citations in the document were spot-checked against the tree at commit a4ba82d.

REVIEWED 2026-08-05. All five section-12 decisions settled; design updated accordingly. Still NOT implemented.

1. HOOK NAMING - approved as proposed: get_state / from_state as classmethods on `class Context` in _commands/<Ctx>/_<Ctx>.py. Not dunders on the application class.
2. LOCATOR HANDLING - approved as proposed: separate get_locator / find_by_locator pair, plus the serialize-time identity self-check find_by_locator(anchor, get_locator(obj)) is obj.
3. VERSION MISMATCH - CHANGED from the draft, and the draft was wrong. The reviewer's point stands: refusing to call from_state on a mismatch makes migration impossible by construction, since the only code that understands an old state shape is the author's. from_state now receives the stored version as a keyword argument and the author migrates or raises. This matches every pattern in section 3 - __setstate__ inspects what it is handed, Django migrations are authored, Avro/protobuf leave reader/writer resolution to the application.
   ONE DELIBERATE DIVERGENCE, FLAGGED FOR SIGN-OFF: the suggestion was to fail fast and crash. The design fails fast - nothing partial is ever applied and every failure is an ERROR - but scopes the failure to the owning session (quarantine the snapshot, continue cold) rather than crashing the process. Reason: restore runs on a live request path during cold rehydration, so a process crash turns one unreadable snapshot into an outage for every unrelated session on that pod, and because the snapshot survives the restart it becomes a crash loop. If a hard process failure is wanted regardless it is a one-line change at the call site and should be settled before implementation.
4. REDACTION - out of scope as directed; filed as fix-cj4 (P1, discovered-from this issue) with the full deny-list draft, the trajectory problem, and the honest statement of what a key-name deny-list cannot catch. Author responsibility is documented in section 6.2: do not attach secrets or PII to contexts or inject them into agent trajectories without strong encryption.
   ONE CARVE-OUT, ALSO FOR SIGN-OFF: fastWorkflow injects the caller's JWT into application context ITSELF - _merge_workflow_context (run_fastapi_mcp/utils.py:253) and _update_http_bearer_token (:260) both set workflow.context["http_bearer_token"]. Under persist-all with zero exclusions the framework would write a credential IT added to disk in the clear, which is not an author mistake and cannot be documented away. The design excludes that one named key. It is a single exclusion, not redaction machinery, and it preserves the intent that key already had.
5. WORKFLOW PROJECTION - approved as proposed: new optional module type _commands/_serialization.py, chosen because messaging_app_3 has no root context to hang it off.

ALSO ADDED, per the request for standard-practice documentation: section 6.1, authoring guidance on versioning and serialization - version from day one, bump on incompatible shape changes, prefer tolerant readers, migrate forward in from_state never in get_state, do not serialize what you can recompute, do not serialize framework objects, keep state JSON-native, rebuild identity explicitly, and round-trip in a test including the locator (equality alone passes while identity is broken). This section is the source for author-facing docs when the mechanism is implemented.

Document: docs/fastworkflow_serialization_hooks_design.md, 457 lines, uncommitted. All nine bd references in it resolve to real issues; all code citations spot-checked against commit a4ba82d.

FOLLOW-UP REVIEW 2026-08-05. Both flagged sign-offs resolved; design updated. Still NOT implemented.

DECISION 3, blast radius - RESOLVED AS "FAIL THE REQUEST". On a from_state refusal the framework quarantines the snapshot, logs ERROR naming both versions, and fails the request with HTTP 500. Rationale accepted: returning 200 with a session that quietly forgot where it was is how the fix-3vy defect stayed invisible in the first place; the caller should see the loss. Because quarantine happens before the failure, the client's retry does not hit the same snapshot - it proceeds cold, so the loss is explicit and bounded to one request. Still not a process crash: restore runs on a request path, and a crash would take down every unrelated session on the pod and then crash-loop on a snapshot that outlives the restart.

DECISION 4, http_bearer_token - the reviewer asked why not ENCRYPT the token during serialization and use that as a normative reference for app developers. Investigated; the answer is that encrypting it would preserve a value that should not be preserved at all, and the token is a better normative example of the OPPOSITE lesson.
Evidence: it is request-scoped data living in a session-scoped container. Every authenticated request re-supplies it - get_session_and_ensure_runtime passes that request's own token (__main__.py:250) and ensure_user_runtime_exists refreshes it on the existing runtime before returning (utils.py:295-297). So persisting it is:
  - unnecessary: the next authenticated request supplies a fresh one regardless;
  - actively harmful: a restored snapshot reinstates the token current when the snapshot was written, which is stale by construction, may be expired, and depending on ordering can overwrite the fresh token the current request just installed;
  - already forbidden: non-negotiable rule 2 of the memory-bounds design (section 1, line 83) says request-scoped credentials are never written to durable channel state.
CONSEQUENCE FOR SCOPE: excluding http_bearer_token is NOT a carve-out from the decision to defer redaction. It implements a rule that predates it. Redaction is a heuristic over values an author chose to store; this is a framework-owned key the framework must not store at all. The two are not the same kind of thing.

ENCRYPTION AS NORMATIVE GUIDANCE - the design now teaches, in priority order: (1) a credential that arrives with a request belongs to that request, so re-supply per request and never checkpoint it; (2) do not attach secrets or PII to contexts or trajectories at all; (3) only when state is both genuinely long-lived AND genuinely secret, encrypt it - with a key that does NOT travel with the ciphertext. A framework-managed key beside the data it protects is the "encrypted at rest, key on the same disk" anti-pattern; real protection is envelope encryption against the deployment's KMS, which fastWorkflow should integrate with rather than own. Reusing the JWT signing key is explicitly rejected as coupling two concerns.
Leading with encryption would normalise persisting secrets when the better answer is usually not to - which is why the token became the worked example for norm (1) rather than a demonstration of encryption.
An optional encrypt/decrypt extension point on `class Serialization` is legitimate for genuinely long-lived secrets and has been folded into fix-cj4, alongside redaction, because both answer the same question and should be designed together.

Document: docs/fastworkflow_serialization_hooks_design.md, uncommitted. Sections changed: 5.1, 6.2, 9 (failure table), 11, 12 (decision table).
APPROVED 2026-08-05. All five decisions settled. Design status is now Approved; implementation may proceed once fix-g03.16 lands (it blocks fix-g03.17).

FINAL RESOLUTIONS on the two items that were open:
- Decision 3 blast radius: FAIL THE REQUEST. Quarantine the snapshot, ERROR naming both versions, HTTP 500. Retry proceeds cold because quarantine happens first. Not a process crash.
- Decision 4 http_bearer_token: EXCLUDED from the default projection. Encrypting it instead was considered and rejected - it would preserve a value that is stale by construction, may be expired, and can overwrite the fresh token the current request just installed. Excluding it implements non-negotiable rule 2 of the memory-bounds design rather than carving an exception out of the redaction deferral.

THE THREE NORMS ARE NOW PUBLISHED AS BEST PRACTICE, not left in the design doc. Added to README.md under "Production deployment -> Handling secrets and PII":
  1. A credential that arrives with a request belongs to that request - re-supply per request, never store in workflow context. The caller's JWT is the worked example: refreshed on every authenticated request, never written to session state.
  2. Keep secrets and PII out of command contexts, workflow context and agent trajectories. Pass an opaque handle (user id, lookup key) and resolve it inside the command, where the value stays in memory and never reaches a parameter, a trace or a trajectory.
  3. If state is both long-lived and genuinely secret, encrypt it with a key that does NOT travel with the ciphertext. A key beside the data it protects moves an audit checkbox, not the exposure. Use the deployment's KMS or secret manager.

THE README ALSO STATES WHAT REACHES DISK TODAY, because the norms are current guidance and not future guidance. Verified in the tree at a4ba82d, independent of any Release B work:
  - command PARAMETERS are written verbatim into conversation_traces on every turn - workflow_execution_context.py:1045-1054 builds the record and append_conversation_turn stores it, and the Release A conversation store persists it to Rdict per turn;
  - the agent's ReAct TRAJECTORY and input_args are written to the pending-session JSON whenever a turn suspends on ask_user - react.py:122-129 export_suspended, serialized by WorkflowExecutionContext.serialize_state and written by DiskSessionStateStore.save.
Both in plaintext. This is pre-existing behaviour, not something Release B introduces; Release B widens it to workflow.context.

KEEP IN STEP: README is the normative copy for authors; section 6.2 of the design doc is the rationale. If one changes, change both.
close_reason: Serialization hook mechanism implemented per the approved design.

title: Evicting a session silently drops its live root command context
description:
MEASURED, not inferred. A workflow that assigns workflow.root_command_context during startup loses it when its session is evicted from the live-session cache, and the next request silently continues in the global context ('*') instead of the application context.

Reproduction (tests/todo_list_workflow, whose _commands/startup.py:12 assigns TodoListManager as the root context):
  1. ensure_user_runtime_exists(run_startup=True) with a direct startup action
     -> root='TodoListManager', current='TodoListManager'
  2. session_manager.evict_live_session(channel); drop the last reference; gc.collect()
  3. ensure_user_runtime_exists(run_startup=False)  <- exactly what get_session_and_ensure_runtime does on the next request (__main__.py:242-251)
     -> root='NoneType', current='*'

Mechanism: Workflow.create() returns a live workflow from _WORKFLOW_REGISTRY (workflow.py:101), but that registry is a WeakValueDictionary (workflow.py:43), so once eviction drops the last strong reference the workflow is collected. The rebuilt Workflow starts with _root_command_context = None (workflow.py:160-161) and cold rehydration deliberately does not re-run startup, so nothing re-establishes it. serialize_state() stores only current_command_context_name, and apply_serialized_state() already logs a DEBUG saying workflow-specific restore is missing (workflow_execution_context.py:402-414).

Blast radius today: reachable only when the live-session cache exceeds MAX_LIVE_SESSIONS (2000), so it is rare in practice but it is silent when it happens - no error, no warning, just commands resolving against the global context. Lowering the cap (memory-bounds Release C) makes eviction routine and would make this common. Affected bundled workflows per the memory-bounds design section 1.4 census: simple_workflow_template (the scaffold new workflows are copied from), messaging_app_2, tests/todo_list_workflow, messaging_app_4 (after set_root_context), messaging_app_3 (after initialize_user). Not affected: messaging_app_1, retail_workflow, hello_world.

Two candidate fixes, neither cheap or side-effect-free:
  (a) Make these sessions restorable - the workflow-declared durable projection of memory-bounds design sections 11.1/11.2 (fix-g03.17 and the strict serializer, record identity and generation work around it). This is the designed answer and is squarely Release B.
  (b) Make them un-evictable - refuse to evict a session whose workflow holds a live root/current/response-generation command-context object, per the design's non-negotiable rule 1 ('a session that cannot be checkpointed safely is NOT evicted'). Small code change in ChannelSessionManager._evict_oldest_if_needed, but it converts silent state loss into a live-session cache that grows without bound for exactly these workflow shapes, which is a real trade and is why section 11.2 makes it part of Release B's eligibility rules rather than a standalone patch.

Do not ship either as a standalone patch on top of Release A: memory-bounds design section 20 prohibits implementing Release B piecemeal, and both fixes are Release B eligibility semantics.
close_reason: Fixed in v2.26.0/v2.27.0 by two independent mechanisms, either alone sufficient. (1) Eviction now refuses: checkpoint.assess() returns not-eligible when project_command_contexts() reports the context is not checkpointable, so a session holding an unserializable root context is PINNED and warned about once per context class instead of being evicted into the global context. (2) The reproduction workflow round-trips: tests/todo_list_workflow now implements get_state/from_state plus the locator pair, and tests/test_workflow_serialization_hooks.py asserts restored.current_command_context is laundry -- the exact nested node by identity, not an equal copy. Verified end to end in tests/test_checkpoint_integration.py, and by the mutation check that removing the assess() guard fails the pinning test.

title: Release A ship: minor release, publish arm A0's slope, keep worker recycling as the interim mitigation
description:
Sections 17 (rollout 1-3) and 20.

Release A is behaviorally atomic on its own: every fix in it is a pure retention bound with no new durable state, no new eviction path and no wire change. It is a MINOR release (default DSPy diagnostic behavior and conversation retention change), not a patch.

Rollout: (1) reproduce the unpatched baseline; (2) pass sections 16.1, 16.2 and the 16.4 DSPy tests plus two full-suite runs, run soak arms A0 and A1 and the latency matrix, then canary while monitoring RSS, conversation bytes, DSPy cache bytes and LLM call counts; (3) keep worker recycling as the SUPPORTED interim mitigation for the unique-channel workload until Release C - a supported posture, not a footnote.

Release notes must state plainly that Release A does NOT close the motivating unique-channel OOM (section 1.2).
The source study's production numbers (~1.758 MB/request before, ~0.032 after, 2000-request soak) are INCONCLUSIVE locally, not rejected, and must not appear in release notes until reproduced with baseline and treatment artifacts.

Do NOT package Releases B or C with A.
acceptance_criteria:
- pyproject.toml minor version bump ships inside the release commit; subject "feat: vX.Y.0 - ...".
- Arm A0's measured slope appears verbatim in the release notes alongside the statement that the motivating OOM is not closed.
- Full suite green twice; no example ___command_info artifacts touched.
notes: Release A code, tests and verification are complete and the ship gates are met: full pytest suite run twice with zero failures (1017 passed, 14 skipped, both runs); version bumped 2.24.1 -> 2.25.0 (minor); arm A0's slope published verbatim in design section 1.2 and in section 16.5.1; worker recycling reaffirmed as the interim mitigation in section 1.2. Remaining is the human action: commit, tag and publish. NOTE for whoever writes the release notes - the durable conversation layout changed (turns moved from an inline list to per-turn Rdict entries). Forward migration is automatic and idempotent, and a rolled-back binary's writes are read correctly on re-upgrade, but a rolled-back binary itself sees conversations as empty. Binary downgrade after this release is not supported for conversation history.
close_reason: Release A shipped: v2.25.0 committed as 0f5be97 and pushed; design of record and both adversarial reviews published as a4ba82d. Arm A0's slope quoted verbatim in design section 1.2, section 16.5.1 and the commit body. Worker recycling reaffirmed as the interim mitigation. Full suite run twice on final code, 1017 passed / 14 skipped / zero failures.

title: Release A verification: soak arms A0/A1 against the real server, plus the latency matrix
description:
Sections 16.5 and 16.6 [R2-22]. Landing order step 5b. Every numeric threshold is PRE-REGISTERED before treatment is measured.

RUN THE REAL SERVER. Revision 2's in-process ASGI harness put client and server in one process and could bypass the dedicated pre-event-loop entrypoint where the DSPy controls must be installed - it could not observe the thing it was meant to gate. The soak launches the actual CLI/Uvicorn server in a separate fresh process and drives it over HTTP.

Method: strictly sequential requests; unique channel and unique ~450 KB payload per request; direct startup action; one warm-up request; BOTH natural-GC and forced-gc.collect() sample series reported separately (forced collection can hide production allocator behavior); several hundred measured requests minimum; second-half least-squares slope; record RSS AND USS AND cgroup memory plus live-heap diagnostics; record session, lock, retained-turn, DSPy history, DSPy trace, DSPy cache entries and bytes, in-memory conversation bytes, and durable-store record counts and bytes; MULTIPLE fresh-process replicates reported with an upper confidence bound rather than a single slope. Capture unpatched baseline and treatment with identical Python, lockfile, payloads, sample count, warm-up, host and replicate count.

ARM A0 - Release A only; function-style workflow; cache limit unchanged at 2000. PRE-REGISTERED EXPECTATION: slope materially below baseline but ABOVE the 0.05 MB/request target, because the session cache still retains every unique channel. RECORDED, NOT GATED. If A0 falsifies that prediction, Release C's urgency drops and this design should be RE-SCOPED rather than continued out of momentum.
ARM A1 - hot single channel; one channel, several hundred request-sized direct actions. Expectation: in-memory conversation bytes plateau; slope at or below target. This arm FAILS without section 8 and is the only arm that tests goal 1 on this workload shape.

Section 16.6 latency, Release A scope: no-eviction live hit; turn completion without overflow; conversation append at depth; LLM call counts with and without the 9.4 cache policy. Gate: no-eviction p50/p95 regresses by less than 5% or measurement noise, whichever is larger.

Report raw samples and slopes. Do NOT replace them with "survived N requests". Do NOT sum ablation deltas as independent shares - the source study's own arms sum to ~2.70 MB/request against a 1.76 MB/request baseline because the retainers share references to the same payload objects.
acceptance_criteria:
- Release A gates on arm A1 (plateau; slope <= 0.05 MB/request) and on all Release A caps holding in arm A0.
- Arm A0's slope is recorded and quoted verbatim in section 1.2 and in the release notes.
- All structurally bounded collections stay at or below their caps; all requests succeed.
- The slope target is treated as a leak budget (0.05 MB/request permits ~78 MB/day at 65 requests/hour), and the acceptance claim is the plateau.
close_reason: Release A soak arms A0 and A1 plus the latency matrix.

title: Release A tests: DSPy structural matrix in isolated .venv subprocesses (16.4)
acceptance_criteria:
- All 9 steps pass against the pinned .venv DSPy 3.2.1.
- The helper is also verified against the minimum allowed DSPy 3.x dependency (section 9.5).
- No network LLM call is made.
close_reason: Release A DSPy structural matrix in isolated venv subprocesses.

title: Release A tests: turn retention (16.1) and conversation bounds (16.2)
description:
Landing order step 5a. Integration tests only - no mocks, real framework components and real test workflows (goal 9). Never train in or delete fastworkflow/examples/*/___command_info (section 16.7).

Section 16.1 deterministic turn tests: >20 completed startup executions retains exactly the newest 20; expired retained startups are removed; non-startup terminal executions are removed during finalization; running and queued executions survive age and count sweeps; long-running work receives a TTL only after completion; task-launch failure rolls back both registry pointers; ordinary identical completed turns are not deduplicated; no store I/O occurs while TurnRegistry._lock is held [R9]; existing single-flight and 409 tests remain unchanged.

Section 16.2 conversation-bound tests: a durable conversation retains ALL turns after the in-memory window has trimmed older ones - THIS TEST MUST FAIL against a naive window that trims before append; incremental save writes only new turns and total bytes over N turns is O(N), not O(N^2); topic and summary generation at shutdown sees the full durable conversation, not the window; /activate_conversation restores the window and sets the high-water mark so the next save does not re-append the conversation; same-channel in-memory history bytes plateau across several hundred request-sized turns.
acceptance_criteria:
- Every section 16.1 and 16.2 case present and passing.
- The durable-retention test is verified to fail against a trim-before-append implementation.
- Full pytest suite run twice with zero failures; no existing test removed, skipped or weakened.
close_reason: Release A implemented and verified; see docs/fastworkflow_memory_bounds_design.md 16.5.1 and 16.6.1.

title: Release A: startup memory-bounds INFO record and memory metrics
description:
Section 17 [R7, R12, R2-20]. Emit exactly one startup INFO record:

memory bounds active: max_live_sessions=2000 (source=default), max_retained_startup_turns=20 (~17 MB at 450 KB payload), turn_retention_seconds=300, max_conversation_turns_in_memory=20, dspy_history=off (asserted), dspy_trace=off (asserted), dspy_memory_cache=200 entries (asserted), dspy_disk_cache=off, dspy_policy_owner=claimed

The byte annotations and (asserted) markers are deliberate: a count cap is unauditable without the payload size, and revision 1 would have logged dspy_trace=off even on a DSPy version that silently ignored the setting. The source= marker on the session cap is required so an operator can see whether a container variable took effect.

Release A runtime logs: DEBUG for turn eviction count and reason; ERROR for DSPy policy drift detected after readiness. Rate-limit warnings per channel and reason, and NEVER log state, payloads, context values or credentials.

METRICS, NOT JUST LOGS: DSPy cache entries and bytes, and in-memory conversation bytes, must be metrics - a rate-limited warning is suppressed exactly when it matters most. (Pinned-session count, quarantined-channel count and durable-store bytes per namespace arrive with Releases B and C.)
acceptance_criteria:
- The startup record is emitted once and reports the resolved max_live_sessions value AND its source.
- Each DSPy control is marked (asserted) only when the section 9.3 structural assertion actually passed.
- DSPy cache entries/bytes and in-memory conversation bytes are exported as metrics and are readable by the section 16.5 soak harness.
close_reason: Release A startup memory-bounds INFO record and retention metrics.

title: Release A: DSPy response-cache policy (200-entry memory cache, disk cache off)
description:
Section 9.4, invariant 24, decision 28 [R2-15]. Landing order step 4b. "Not configured" is not a policy.

REPRODUCED: under the 9.1 history/trace policy, four unique Predict calls with litellm_completion replaced below LM.forward leave GLOBAL_HISTORY / LM history / settings.trace at 0/0/0 but the DSPy RESPONSE CACHE at 4 entries. Installed defaults are memory_max_entries=1000000 and disk_size_limit_bytes=30000000000 (30 GB); dspy.LM defaults cache=True and get_lm() never overrides it (fastworkflow/utils/dspy_utils.py:42-69). The server therefore runs with a one-million-entry in-memory response cache that revision 2's policy did not touch.

Work, in server_memory.py at the same entrypoint and ordering as section 9.2 (configure_cache REPLACES the global cache object, so it must run before any LM is created):
dspy.configure_cache(enable_memory_cache=True, memory_max_entries=SERVER_DSPY_MEMORY_CACHE_ENTRIES, enable_disk_cache=False)
with SERVER_DSPY_MEMORY_CACHE_ENTRIES = 200.

Disk cache off because 30 GB is not a sane default for a container, this design already has a durable-growth problem, and DSPy's disk cache uses pickle (configure_cache(restrict_pickle=False) by default), which conflicts with decision 10's no-pickle stance.
The 200 figure is a STARTING POINT (~90 MB worst case at 450 KB) sized to keep worst-case retention comparable to the live-session budget - not a derived number. Section 16.6 measures entry BYTES and the figure is revisited against that measurement.
Cost accepted and measured, not waved away: in the motivating unique-channel workload the cache never hits, so disabling disk costs nothing; in a repeated-prompt workload it means more provider calls after a restart. Disabling the response cache entirely was REJECTED because parameter extraction and NLU issue structurally similar prompts within a session.

DO NOT reuse fastworkflow/utils/dspy_cache_utils.py:21-25 - it passes enable_litellm_cache, which configure_cache no longer accepts on DSPy 3.2.1 (TypeError). It has no in-process callers, so nothing depends on it, but it cannot be reused and is not evidence that cache control works.
acceptance_criteria:
- Section 16.4 step 9: response-cache entries stay at or below SERVER_DSPY_MEMORY_CACHE_ENTRIES and the disk cache is not written.
- The cache probe patches BELOW LM.forward with a REAL FUNCTION carrying __module__ and __qualname__: the cache wrapper computes f"{fn.__module__}.{fn.__qualname__}" (dspy/clients/cache.py:246), so a unittest.mock.Mock raises AttributeError before the cache is ever reached.
- Section 16.6: additional provider calls with the policy are within the pre-registered budget, or the 200-entry figure is revised against measured entry bytes.
close_reason: Release A DSPy response-cache policy shipped.

title: Release A: server_memory.py - DSPy history/trace policy, installed pre-event-loop, asserted and owned
description:
Sections 9.1-9.3, 9.5; invariants 13, 14, 24 [R7, R2-19]. Landing order step 4a. New focused module fastworkflow/run_fastapi_mcp/server_memory.py.

POLICY (9.1): dspy.settings.configure(disable_history=True, max_trace_size=0, trace=[]). disable_history=True is required - max_history_size=0 alone still permits DSPy's separate GLOBAL_HISTORY append. max_trace_size=0 is the predictor-trace off switch; a fresh empty trace also releases pre-start trace references. Clear GLOBAL_HISTORY IMMEDIATELY BEFORE installing the policy - the helper cannot find arbitrary old per-LM histories, so ordering is part of the contract.
VERIFIED: in the production call shape (Predict inside dspy.context inside a ThreadPoolExecutor, stubbing only LM.forward) baseline reached 4/4/4 entries in GLOBAL_HISTORY, the LM's history and settings.trace; with the policy all three stayed at 0/0/0. Read sites: dspy/clients/base_lm.py:98 and :223; dspy/predict/predict.py:228.

TIMING AND OWNERSHIP (9.2): do NOT make the first configure call inside FastAPI's async lifespan. VERIFIED unsafe: calling the proposed configuration in one asyncio.run() and then from a second async task raises DSPy's owner-task RuntimeError. Install synchronously from the dedicated server entrypoint before uvicorn creates the event loop and before any server LM is created. The helper is idempotent; if a different thread or task owns incompatible DSPy global settings, FAIL STARTUP with an actionable error rather than advertising a known leak. Claiming process-global ownership is safe because there is NO dspy.configure() or dspy.settings.configure() call anywhere in the fastworkflow package (VERIFIED) - request-path code uses only dspy.context(...).

STRUCTURAL ASSERTION (9.3): configuring is not evidence. Settings.configure performs NO key validation (it is main_thread_config[k] = v), and pyproject.toml:50 allows dspy = "^3.0.1", so on a 3.0.x that does not read these keys the policy is a silent no-op while the startup log cheerfully says dspy_history=off. So, after installing and before readiness: (1) clear GLOBAL_HISTORY; (2) install the policy; (3) make one throwaway Predict call through a stub LM.forward boundary - no network call, no provider credentials, no cost; (4) assert GLOBAL_HISTORY, the stub LM's history and settings.trace are all still empty; (5) on failure fail readiness with an error naming the installed DSPy version and the settings.

OWNERSHIP BEYOND THE PROBE [R2-19]: REPRODUCED - synchronous configure() claims the owner thread but leaves the async owner unset (dspy/dsp/utils/settings.py:117-145), so the first async task on that thread flips disable_history back to False and max_trace_size to 10000 while the startup probe stays green in the logs. Attribute assignment (dspy.settings.x = y) also routes through configure() (settings.py:87-91). Therefore: claim the async owner deliberately before accepting traffic so any later async configure() raises DSPy's own ownership error; re-assert the policy at readiness-probe time so drift becomes an unready pod rather than a silent leak; ERROR-log drift.

WORKER AND RELOAD MODEL [R2-19]: spawned Uvicorn workers do not inherit the parent's globals, so either each worker process runs the bootstrap or multi-worker and --reload modes are explicitly refused. The entrypoint must not silently support a configuration in which half the processes have no policy.

Scope (invariant 13, section 9.5): run_fastapi_mcp only. Training, build, refine and CLI entrypoints are unchanged. dspy.inspect_history() intentionally has no server-request history; fastWorkflow's bounded command traces and logs remain the server diagnostic surface. Verify the helper against the MINIMUM allowed DSPy 3.x dependency as well as the installed 3.2.1 before release.
acceptance_criteria:
- Section 16.4 DSPy structural steps 1-8 pass in an isolated .venv/bin/python subprocess, in the production call shape (Predict inside dspy.context(lm=..., adapter=...) inside a ThreadPoolExecutor worker).
- The startup assertion and the test assert the SAME thing, so the runtime guarantee and the test cannot drift.
- A post-readiness async configure() is rejected, and the readiness probe reports unready when the policy has drifted.
- No network LLM call is added (goal 7).
close_reason: Release A: server_memory.py DSPy policy shipped.

title: Release A: weak creation-lock mapping
description:
Section 7. Landing order step 3.

VERIFIED - creation locks grow with unique channel IDs: ChannelSessionManager._creation_locks is a strong dictionary with no removal path (run_fastapi_mcp/utils.py:689-701). A fresh local reproduction requested locks for 300 unique IDs and retained 300.

Work: replace with weakref.WeakValueDictionary[str, asyncio.Lock]. asyncio.Lock is weak-referenceable on supported Python; the caller and queued waiters hold strong references while the lock matters, and the entry drops once all release. VERIFIED locally: a WeakValueDictionary entry persists while any holder or waiter has a strong reference and drops to zero entries once all release.

DO NOT manually pop an apparently unlocked lock (section 20 prohibition list). A waiter may have been awakened but not yet resumed; deleting the shared lock in that window lets a new caller create a second lock and defeats single-flight creation. Weak values also clean up failed creations that never reach an eviction path.
acceptance_criteria:
- Creation locks disappear after successful AND failed creation.
- Concurrent cold requests for one channel still create exactly one runtime (section 16.4).
close_reason: Release A: weak creation-lock mapping shipped.

title: Release A: bound terminal TurnExecution retention and roll back failed task launches
description:
Section 6, invariant 17 [R9, R13]. Landing order step 2.

VERIFIED - terminal turns are retained forever: TurnRegistry._by_key receives every execution (run_fastapi_mcp/turns.py:202-213); clear_active() removes only _active_by_channel (:216-224); ttl_expires_at is never assigned, so evict_terminal() is a no-op (:226-243). A fresh local reproduction inserted 300 terminal executions; eviction removed 0.

Retention policy (section 6.1): only /initialize looks up a terminal execution by turn_key (__main__.py:689-705). Retain terminal kind == "initialize_startup"; remove other terminal kinds during finalization; preserve the local TurnExecution reference held by the completing request so response rendering is unaffected.

Terminal transition (section 6.2), in _run_turn's finally path: (1) stamp finished_at; (2) set exec_state=DONE; (3) call clear_active(channel_id, turn_key) and, INSIDE THAT SAME LOCK BLOCK: remove the execution immediately if its kind is not collectable; otherwise assign ttl_expires_at = finished_at + TURN_RETENTION_SECONDS (300) once; remove expired retained startups; if more than MAX_RETAINED_STARTUP_TURNS (= 20; ~17 MB at a 450 KB payload) remain, remove the oldest by (finished_at or created_at, turn_key); (4) set done_event; (5) AFTER the registry lock is released, request live-session trimming.

[R13] The clear_active call and "remove the matching active pointer" are ONE step, not two. An implementer following a two-step list would either remove the pointer twice or re-enter registry._lock inside clear_active - and asyncio.Lock is not reentrant, so that reading DEADLOCKS inside a turn's finally block. The sweep contains no await.
Step 5 is ordered explicitly because trimming performs store I/O; doing it inside the lock block would hold registry._lock across a synchronous write and block start_or_get_active - that is, every turn submission on every channel (invariant 17 [R9]).

Section 6.3 task-launch rollback: start_or_get_active() inserts the execution and active pointer before invoking run_turn(execution). Preserve that construction order, but if task creation raises synchronously, remove both inserted pointers before re-raising - otherwise a rare launch failure creates an immortal non-terminal entry that retention must never evict (invariant 1).

Use constructor injection for the constants so tests are deterministic.

Scope note [R2-16]: retention is justified SOLELY by the live-runtime re-poll path. There is no GET /turns/{turn_key} route, InitializationRequest carries no prior turn_key, and cold /initialize returns tokens only - so revision 2's cross-eviction recoverability claim is withdrawn. The count binds before the 300 s window in a burst of 21 startups, and that is an accepted limitation, not a sizing target. Do not generalize terminal deduplication to ordinary completed turns: two identical user queries may be intentional.
acceptance_criteria:
Section 16.1:
- More than 20 completed startup executions retains exactly the newest 20.
- Expired retained startups are removed.
- Non-startup terminal executions are removed during finalization.
- RUNNING and QUEUED executions survive age and count sweeps (invariant 1).
- Long-running work receives a TTL only after completion.
- Task-launch failure rolls back both registry pointers.
- Ordinary identical completed turns are not deduplicated.
- No store I/O occurs while TurnRegistry._lock is held.
- Existing single-flight and 409 tests remain unchanged.
close_reason: Release A implemented and verified. See docs/fastworkflow_memory_bounds_design.md sections 16.5.1 and 16.6.1 for measured results.

title: Release A: topic/summary and /activate_conversation must read the durable record, not the window
description:
Section 8.3 [R2-11]. Landing order step 1c. These are required parts of the windowing change, not optional polish.

1. finalize_conversations_on_shutdown and generate_topic_and_summary operate on extract_turns_from_history (run_fastapi_mcp/__main__.py:308). Once history is windowed they must read the durable conversation record instead, or topics silently become "topic of the last 20 turns".
2. /activate_conversation already replaces history wholesale (__main__.py:1471-1472). It must load the windowed tail AND set the high-water mark accordingly, or the next incremental save re-appends the whole conversation.
acceptance_criteria:
- Topic and summary generation at shutdown sees the full durable conversation, not the window (section 16.2).
- /activate_conversation restores the window and sets the high-water mark so the next save does not re-append the conversation (section 16.2).
close_reason: Release A implemented and verified; see docs/fastworkflow_memory_bounds_design.md 16.5.1 and 16.6.1.

title: Release A: bound in-memory conversation history to 20 turns (invariant 23)
description:
Sections 8.1 and 8.3, invariant 23 [R2-11]. Landing order step 1b.

GOAL 1 IS FALSE TODAY on this workload and no cache bound touches it. append_conversation_turn() appends unconditionally to dspy.History.messages (workflow_execution_context.py:437-451) while only the last five entries are ever read, by _refine_user_query (:1046-1059). Nothing trims older entries; history is cleared only by an explicit /new_conversation and is persisted and restored wholesale. A single hot channel issuing bounded 450 KB direct actions therefore grows one request-sized entry per completed request even when terminal executions are removed immediately, the session count is one, DSPy history and trace are off, and no object context pins additional channels. The direct-action path appends the record itself (:1037-1039), so growth is proportional to payload, not to a summary.

Work: after a turn is durably recorded (A1), trim conversation_history.messages to the newest MAX_CONVERSATION_TURNS_IN_MEMORY (= 20; ~9 MB per channel at a 450 KB payload; only 5 entries are read, so 20 is 4x margin). The cap is per-channel, so the aggregate scales with live sessions. restore_history_from_turns is handed the same windowed tail rather than the full conversation.

What this does NOT buy (section 8.4): it does not help the motivating unique-channel workload, where each channel has exactly one conversation turn. There the entry is retained because the SESSION is retained, and only Release C reclaims it.
acceptance_criteria:
- Same-channel in-memory conversation bytes plateau across several hundred request-sized turns (section 16.2; soak arm A1).
- A durable conversation retains ALL turns after the window has trimmed older ones - this test must FAIL against a naive window that trims before append.
- _refine_user_query behavior is unchanged (it reads the last 5).
close_reason: Completed in Release A implementation.

title: Release A: durable conversation append + high-water mark
description:
Section 8.2 [R2-11 absorption]. Landing order step 1a - this must land BEFORE the in-memory window.

save_conversation_incremental extracts ALL turns from in-memory history (run_fastapi_mcp/utils.py:798) and save_conversation_turns assigns conv["turns"] = turns (conversation_store.py:264-269) - a full replace, not an append. Two consequences:
1. Trimming memory first would DELETE durable turns on the next save, converting a memory leak into data loss - the exact trade this design refuses everywhere else.
2. The write volume is O(n^2): turn n rewrites all n turns, so a 450 KB/turn conversation writes ~n x 450 KB on every turn. That is a latency and durable-growth defect independent of memory, and it is why this step is worth doing on its own.

Work:
- add append_conversation_turns(conversation_id, new_turns) to conversation_store.py, replacing the full-list rewrite;
- add a per-runtime high-water mark of turns already durably recorded;

acceptance_criteria:

title: Bounded memory for run_fastapi_mcp (Releases A/B/C)
description:
Implement docs/fastworkflow_memory_bounds_design.md revision 3 (design of record; code-verified; adversarially reviewed twice; verified against fastWorkflow 2.24.1 @ c206a813, DSPy 3.2.1 in .venv).

run_fastapi_mcp retains request-sized objects in process-lifetime structures and uses a live-session default that is too large for payload-heavy workflows. Lowering that cache limit exposes a correctness problem: evicting a runtime can silently drop application state. Revision 2's single behaviorally-atomic release is WITHDRAWN (decision 23, review section 5). The work ships as three separately gated releases:

A - universal memory bounds. Bound terminal TurnExecution records; store creation locks weakly; bound per-conversation in-memory history; disable DSPy history and predictor trace; make an explicit DSPy response-cache decision. No change to MAX_LIVE_SESSIONS, no new persistence, no new eviction path, no wire change. Depends on nothing. Minor release.
B - session checkpoint protocol. Runtime leases and a unified turn lifecycle for streaming; an explicit workflow-declared snapshot capability; complete or pinned continuation state; a generation-stamped, identity-bound composite commit; request-scoped credential handling; namespace lifecycle and a fleet-version protocol. Depends on A.
C - lower the live-session default. MAX_LIVE_SESSIONS 2000 -> 50 with an operator-reachable resolver. Depends on B.

The ordering is dependency, not preference: lowering the cache limit is what makes eviction routine; eviction is what makes state preservation necessary; state preservation is where all 14 blocking round-2 findings live.

THREE NON-NEGOTIABLE RULES ACROSS ALL RELEASES:
1. A session that cannot be checkpointed safely is NOT evicted. The LRU may remain over target indefinitely. Never trade an allocation problem for silent application-state loss.
2. Request-scoped credentials are never written to durable channel state and never installed into shared workflow state outside an accepted turn's lifecycle.
3. DSPy memory controls are installed before the server event loop and request worker threads start - not from the FastAPI lifespan task - and their being IN FORCE is asserted, not assumed, and re-asserted against post-readiness override.

STATED UP FRONT (section 1.2): Release A does NOT close the motivating production OOM. That deployment issues a unique channel_id per request at a 450 KB payload and was OOM-killed at a 1 GB container limit after roughly 200 requests; at the unchanged 2000-session default the cache never reaches its limit in that window, so it retains every channel. Only Release C reclaims them. Worker recycling remains the supported interim mitigation.

CONDITIONAL SCOPE (section 1.4): Release C's bound is conditional on workflow shape. Five bundled workflows including simple_workflow_template - the scaffold new workflows are copied from - assign a command-context object and are therefore PINNED and never evicted. A pinned workflow cannot meet the shipping gate and must not be described as bounded.

References: design docs/fastworkflow_memory_bounds_design.md (rev 3); round-1 review ..._review.md (R1-R15); round-2 review ..._review_round_2.md (R2-1..R2-22, 14 S1 / 7 S2 / 1 S3). Landing order: section 15.1. Verification: section 16. Decision log: section 18. Traceability: section 21.
acceptance_criteria:
- Release A ships on its own evidence with soak arm A0's slope published rather than elided.
- Releases B and C are never packaged with A, and C never precedes B.
- Decisions 18, 23, 24 and 25 are resolved before any Release B code lands.
- No shortcut from the section 20 prohibition list is reintroduced (manual creation-lock pruning; early return on empty context; default=str anywhere in the path; evicting after a failed state write; persisting credentials; first-configuring DSPy inside the async lifespan; treating configure() or a one-time probe as proof; deriving startup-already-ran from in-process retention; a sampled boolean as the eviction predicate; a snapshot silently outranking redeployed configuration; inferring eligibility from negative checks; two independent writes called one transaction; gating on a slope while durable storage grows without bound).
notes:
ALL THREE RELEASES SHIPPED AND VERIFIED (2026-08-06). Left open deliberately: the only remaining child, fix-g03.25, is a decision-26 deferral rather than unfinished release work, and closing an epic over it is an owner call.

A - v2.25.0, commit 0f5be97. Universal retention bounds: durable conversation append with a per-runtime high-water mark, a 20-turn in-memory window (invariant 23), bounded terminal turn retention with task-launch rollback, weak creation locks, and a DSPy memory policy installed before the event loop, structurally asserted and owned.

B - v2.26.0, commit b397d10. The session checkpoint protocol: manager-owned eviction leases (invariants 19/20), streaming routed through turn admission, one strict serializer at the WEC boundary with default=str removed everywhere, identity-bound records published as one generation with a commit record, a durable startup state machine, three-way launch reconciliation, request-scoped credentials installed only under the accepted turn, and the author serialization-hook mechanism with all five pinned bundled workflows implemented.

C - v2.27.0, commit 1938215. Live-session cap lowered 2000 -> 50 behind an OS-first resolver, with checkpoint retention (fix-jtr) as its blocker.

THE MOTIVATING OOM IS CLOSED. The unique-channel 450 KB workload measured +1.339 MB/request unpatched, +0.495 after Release A, and +0.011 after Release C. The durable namespace reaches a plateau (56.0 MB across 1592 channels at 3500 requests, with byte decreases as reclamation fires) rather than a slower rate of growth, which is what section 16.5 requires. Every gate met. Full suite 1297 passed / 14 skipped / zero failures, run twice per release.

EIGHT PRODUCTION DEFECTS WERE FOUND BY THE TEST MATRICES RATHER THAN BY READING THE CODE, all fixed: a failed checkpoint write aborted the whole eviction sweep; the startup commit was wired only into the streaming path so /initialize never reached it; admission closure was registry-only, so the manager kept creating sessions during shutdown and a mid-creation channel was invisible to the drain; graceful shutdown closed runtimes without publishing their checkpoints; the strict serializer caught a test persisting a stringified MagicMock; and three more inside the checkpoint store found by its own mutation testing.

REMAINING FOLLOW-UPS, none blocking:
- fix-g03.25 - complete logical-turn and CME continuation serialization. This is why awaiting_user and continuation sessions are PINNED in Release B v1 (decision 26): the suspended snapshot does not carry the turn accumulator, and pinning avoids making a known defect routine without pretending to have fixed it. Note it does not help multi-pod, where another pod still cold-rehydrates.
- fix-cj4 - redaction of secrets and PII, plus the optional encrypt/decrypt extension point.
- fix-3vy - the pre-existing eviction context-loss bug. Release B removed the reachable path for hooked workflows; an un-hooked one now pins instead of losing state.
- fix-wi3 - test_session_not_found_errors is latency-flaky against a real LLM.

DOC STATE: design sections 11.1 and 11.2 are superseded by docs/fastworkflow_serialization_hooks_design.md (decision 25 was reversed) and are retained for provenance. The header says so. A full revision 4 that merges the hooks model into section 11 has NOT been written.
close_reason: All three releases shipped and verified: A (universal memory bounds) in v2.25.0, B (session checkpoint protocol) in v2.26.0, C (lowered live-session cap plus checkpoint retention) in v2.27.0. All 28 children closed; the last, fix-g03.25, shipped in v2.28.0 and reversed decision 26 by completing the suspended-state serialization and removing the awaiting_user pin. Measured on the same harness: +1.339 MB/request unpatched, +0.495 after Release A, +0.011 after Release C, with the durable namespace reaching a plateau at 56.0 MB across 1592 channels rather than growing without bound. Design of record is docs/fastworkflow_memory_bounds_design.md revision 4, which reconciles the design with what was actually built. Follow-ups tracked separately: fix-cj4 (redaction), fix-6b4 (pending-blob retention), fix-4od (schema migration, fail-closed half already done).

title: Define lifecycle for the channel checkpoint namespace
description: R2-17: fix-6b4 covers orphaned suspended-session blobs only. The Release B checkpoint namespace (workflow context + conversation records) has no TTL, reaper, inspect/quarantine/delete API, or generation-safe channel reuse. Required before Release C lowers MAX_LIVE_SESSIONS, because unique-channel workloads write a snapshot per request that is never read again.
close_reason: Checkpoint namespace lifecycle implemented in fastworkflow/checkpoint_store.py (206 tests, 15/15 mutations killed). RetentionPolicy states the policy rather than hiding a TTL (decision 16): an age window plus max_channels/max_bytes caps, with describe() printing the resulting byte ceiling because a count cap is unauditable without it. The reaper is INVOKED, never scheduled - no thread inside the store, since a background sweeper would be a second writer per channel (invariant 15); the server drives it from a lifespan task every 300s and names every live or leased channel as protected. Crash safety is publish's prepare-then-flip run backwards: reclamation makes a complete channel invisible with one rename, so no interrupted pass leaves a readable partial generation, and debris sweeping runs first. Operator API: inspect/list_channels, quarantine/list_quarantine_entries, delete, reset, reap(dry_run=), stats(). Channel reuse is safe two ways - delete is one atomic rename so nothing of the old lineage survives to adopt, and reset records a generation floor so numbers never repeat. stats().total_bytes_physical is what the section 16.5 plateau gate measures. Stated limits: nothing is reclaimed unless reap is called; growth between passes is unbounded; one record's size is unbounded; caps are per namespace; a fingerprint that changes every deploy creates a namespace whose predecessor is reclaimed only by age.
